summary.text: The margin of error is a statistic that expresses how much random sampling error there is in a survey's results.
The larger it is, the less confident you should be that a poll's result matches what a simultaneous census of the whole population would show.
As long as the sampling fraction is small, it is essentially the same whether the population is a school, a city, a state or a country.

facts.label: Meaning
facts.value: The amount of random sampling error in a survey's results

facts.label: Default level
facts.value: 95% when no confidence level is given

facts.label: Near the extremes
facts.value: Approaches ±0% as a percentage nears 0% or 100%

facts.label: Population size
facts.value: Essentially unchanged from a school to a country if the sampling fraction is small

items.prompt: Two polls use the same method and the same small sampling fraction, one of a school and one of a whole country. How do their margins of error compare?

options.label: The country's is far larger because it has more people
The school's is far larger because it is closer-knit
They are essentially the same
Neither poll can have a margin of error

items.explain: For a given sampling method the margin of error is essentially the same whatever the population size, as long as the sampling fraction is small.

items.prompt: Poll A reports a larger margin of error than Poll B. What should you conclude?

options.label: Less confidence that A's result matches a census of everyone
A's result is certainly wrong and should be thrown out
A must have surveyed more people than B did
A was surely run with a clearly biased method

items.explain: The larger the margin of error, the less confidence one should have that the poll result would reflect a census of the whole population.

items.prompt: As a poll's reported percentage gets very close to 0% or 100%, what happens to its margin of error?

options.label: It grows, because small shares are noisier
It stays the same for every percentage
It stops existing once the share is tiny
It shrinks toward zero

items.explain: A given percentage's margin of error approaches ±0% as the percentage approaches the extremes of 0% or 100%.

items.prompt: A poll report states a margin of error of 3 points but never mentions a confidence level. Which level should you assume?
items.explain: If no explicit confidence level is given, the most commonly used level is 95%.

items.prompt: A survey asks about a trait that differs from person to person, and it covers only part of the population. Can its margin of error be zero?

options.label: Yes, if the sample is chosen carefully enough
Yes, if the sample is large enough
No, it is positive when part is left out and the measure varies
Only if every person is asked twice

items.explain: The margin of error is positive whenever a population is incompletely sampled and the outcome measure varies.

items.prompt: A lab report gives a measured length with a margin of error. Outside of surveys, what might that margin describe?

options.label: Observational error in the measured quantity
How many people were surveyed for the report
The share of respondents who said yes
The size of the full population

items.explain: The term is often used outside surveys to indicate observational error in reporting measured quantities.

paragraphs.heading: The plus-or-minus on a poll
paragraphs.text: The margin of error is a number that says how much random sampling error a survey's results contain. A bigger margin means you should trust less that the poll matches what a census of the whole population, taken at the same moment, would find. Any time only part of a population is asked and the answers vary, the margin of error is above zero. Outside surveys, the phrase is also used for observational error in reported measurements.

paragraphs.heading: Imagining many repeat polls
paragraphs.text: Picture a yes-or-no poll of n people, drawn from a much larger population, that finds a share p saying yes. We want to know how close p is to the true share without asking everyone. Suppose we ran the same poll again and again on fresh samples. The results would be expected to form a normal distribution around the true but unknown share, and the margin of error is the distance within which a stated percentage of them should fall.

paragraphs.heading: Where the 95% comes from
paragraphs.text: By the 68-95-99.7 rule, 95% of those repeat results should land within about two standard deviations of the true value. That range is called the confidence interval, and half its width is the margin of error at a 95% confidence level. When a poll does not state a confidence level, 95% is the one most often used. A margin reported at 95% can be turned into one at 99% by multiplying it by about 1.3.

paragraphs.heading: Sample size and the formula
paragraphs.text: In general the margin of error equals a z-score times the standard error, written MOE _(1−2α) = z_(1−α) × √(σ²/n). At 95% confidence the z-score is about 2, giving MOE _0.95 ≈ 2 × √(σ²/n). The smaller the sample size n, the wider the margin. For a yes-or-no poll, the standard error is roughly √((p (1 − p))/n).

paragraphs.heading: Population size hardly matters
paragraphs.text: These formulas assume an endlessly large population, so they depend only on the sample size n, not on the population size N. Sampling theory says that assumption is reasonable when the sample is a small fraction of the population. So a given sampling method has about the same margin of error whether the population is a school, a city, a state or a whole country. As a reported share gets close to 0% or 100%, its margin of error shrinks toward zero.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a close race
paragraphs.text: Imagine a poll of 1013 people that puts three options at 46%, 42% and 12%. The margin usually reported is the one for the 46% figure, because it is nearest to 50%. But talk of a statistical tie, or dead heat, is about something else: not how accurate each number is, but whether the ranking of the options is right.
